title: TB6-12035
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellants are also requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) substitute a positive decision.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), and her minor son, XXXX XXXX, both citizens of the People's Republic of China, are appealing the decisions of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), denying their claims for refugee protection. They have not submitted any new evidence in support of their appeals, however they are asking for a further hearing before the RPD. The Appellants are also requesting that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) substitute a positive decision.
Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD. This appeal is dismissed. Background

The Appellants' claims are based on the Appellant's Falun Gong (FG) practice in China. She was married in 2003 and that same year the minor Appellant was born on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2003. However, in 2011, she discovered that her husband had an affair with another woman, but he was not willing to grant her a divorce at that time. She last saw her husband in XXXX 2012, when he disappeared.

In XXXX 2013, the Appellant's friend, XXXX XXXX, introduced her to FG. Her friend explained that this would assist in relaxation and improving her health following the separation from her husband. Although the Appellant initially was hesitant given the illegality of this practice, her friend assured her of the safety precautions in place. She therefore joined the group every Saturday and practiced at home daily.

In XXXX 2014, the Appellant went to Japan. Upon her return she was required to work overtime, and as a result, she did not attend the group practice. In the afternoon, she received a telephone call from her mother-in-law at her workplace informing her that the Public Security Bureau (PSB) had been looking for her and demanding that she report to the police station immediately. She was also told that all four of her co-practitioners had been arrested. As a result, the Appellant went to hide at the home of her old schoolmate, XXXX XXXX XXXX. While in hiding, the PSB returned and threatened her parents-in-law. At this point, the Appellant decided to contact a snakehead to assist her and her son to escape to Canada. The Appellant alleges that the other members of her group remain in detention.

The Appellant has made submissions on the Role of the RAD, which are in line with the earlier decision in Huruglica1 However, the RAD finds that the recent Federal Court of Appeal decision, in Huruglica,2 provides us with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by a specialized tribunal such as the RAD to decisions of a first-level administrative tribunal. The justices stated at paragraph 103: [103] I conclude from my statutory analysis that with respect to findings of fact (and mixed fact and law) such as the one involved here, which raised no issue of credibility of oral evidence, the RAD is to review RPD decisions applying the correctness standard. Thus, after carefully considering the RPD decision, the RAD carries out its own analysis of the record to determine whether, as submitted by the appellant, the RPD erred. Having done this, the RAD is to provide a final determination, either by confirming the RPD decision or setting it aside and substituting its own determination of the merits of the refugee claim. It is only when the RAD is of the opinion that it cannot provide such a final determination without hearing the oral evidence presented to the RPD that the matter can be referred back to the RPD for redetermination. No other interpretation of the relevant statutory provisions is reasonable. SUBMISSIONS BY THE APPELLANT * Did the RPD ignore evidence properly before it? * Did the RPD make unwarranted implausibility findings? * Did the RPD fail to conduct a proper sur place analysis? Reason for joining FG

The Appellant provided no corroborative evidence with respect to the disappearance of her husband in 2012, notwithstanding the fact that the RPD had requested this from her, given the concern surrounding the fact that she had left China without permission for her son to travel. Although the RPD concluded that in the absence of evidence, it would not exclude the Appellant on this basis, it considered this lack of evidence with respect to the issue of why she had joined FG. The RPD rejected the Appellant's explanation that no one was sufficiently literate to write on her behalf and therefore no letters or documentation could be provided to explain that the Appellant's husband had disappeared and no one knew of his whereabouts. Since this was allegedly the reason the Appellant turned to the practice of FG, the hearing was held over 1 1/2 years after she initiated the claim, and the RPD had requested this information, the RPD drew a negative inference in this regard.

The Appellant has made no submissions in this regard. However, the RAD is charged with conducting an independent assessment of the entire record. In this regard, the RAD concurs that the lack of this corroborative evidence calls into question the assertion of why the Appellant turned to an illegal cult, knowing the consequences if discovered. The RAD finds it is noteworthy that even for the purpose of this appeal, the Appellant provided no new evidence in this regard, although admittedly, since given the opportunity to do so at the RPD hearing, the RAD may well have not admitted it. Practice of FG

The RPD noted that the Appellant testified that she performed the five exercises, and read the book Zhuan Falun. She further testified that she attended group practice twice weekly and practiced at home and read Zhuan Falun the other days. The Appellant was asked to explain why her Basis of Claim (BOC) stated that she practiced with the group only on Saturdays. She responded that it was the staff at her lawyer's office who told her to state this in her BOC, but it was incorrect. Later, she corrected this by stating that the staff may have missed it. Given the internally inconsistent evidence, the RPD drew a negative inference.

The Appellant has not made any submissions with respect to the foregoing inconsistencies. However, the RAD must take into account the credibility of the Appellant when assessing the entire record. Since the study and practice of FG is the impetus of the claim, the RAD concurs with the RPD that a negative inference must be drawn. To simply blame staff, when the instructions are clear in the BOC and the Appellant is represented by competent counsel, has no merit. Arrest of four co-practitioners

The Appellant testified that she asked the friend with whom she was hiding to go to her co-practitioner XXXX home and ask her mother about her co-practitioners; however, this was not mentioned in her BOC. Her explanation for this omission was again that the staff at her counsel's office told her there was no need to state this. However, the RPD noted that the BOC states that the Appellant discovered the arrest of her co-practitioners when she received a telephone call from her mother-in-law telling her that the police had informed her that the Appellant must turn herself in to the police station and that all four practitioners had been arrested, causing her to then hide at her friend's home. The RPD found that it was not reasonable or plausible that the staff at her lawyer's office would encourage her to omit this information in the BOC, as the instructions clearly state that everything that is important ought to be included, and therefore, it drew a negative inference.

The Appellant has made no submissions with respect to the foregoing, yet the fact that all of her fellow practitioners were allegedly detained is an integral portion of the evidence. The RAD concurs with the RPD that it was not reasonable for the Appellant to blame staff at her lawyer's office for omissions in her BOC, given the instructions and the assistance of a competent counsel. Copy of Zhuan Falun

The Appellant was asked at the hearing what happened to her copy of Zhuan Falun. She responded that it was hidden in a secret place at the practice site. However, given her earlier testimony, that she read this book at home daily, and only went to the practice site on the weekend, she was asked to explain the discrepancy. Her response that she finished reading the book and then hid it there, was rejected by the RPD for the following reasons: the omission from her testimony that she had completed reading the book, and given its complexity, the RPD found it unreasonable and implausible that she would cease to study it after reading the text once, particularly when her earlier testimony was that she read the book daily. As a result of this inconsistent testimony, the RPD drew a further negative inference.

The RAD concurs with the RPD that this inconsistency calls into question whether or not the Appellant ever had a copy of Zhuan Falun or whether or not she had read it. Appellant's residency and her place of hiding

The Appellant allegedly resided at a different address as of XXXX 2012; however, this address was not included in her Schedule A form. Her explanation that she had not officially moved out was rejected by the RPD. Moreover, when initially asked why she remained at this address when she allegedly was in hiding, she replied that she stayed there because she could not locate a hiding place. Later she changed her testimony to indicate that she stayed with her friend at the same address but in a second building. Given that the Appellant allegedly lived and then went into hiding at the same address, and she had not provided any corroborative evidence in this regard, the RPD drew a further negative inference and found, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant did not go into hiding in XXXX 2014.

This is a significant part of the Appellant's allegations. She allegedly went into hiding, and following this felt the need for a smuggler to facilitate her departure from China. When the issue of where the Appellant was hiding is called into question, and a satisfactory explanation is not proffered, the RAD concurs with the RPD, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant was not in hiding. Son's ability to attend school while Appellant was in hiding

The RPD found no evidence that the Appellant's son had been expelled from school. It made this finding, however, in conjunction with the fact that none of her family members had suffered any ill-effects, notwithstanding the alleged 7 or 8 visits by the PSB.

The Appellant submits that her affidavit clarifies this issue. She states that she misunderstood the question and that her son has, in fact, been expelled from school after she began to have problems with the PSB.

The RAD finds that with respect to the Appellant's assertion now in her Affidavit that her son was expelled from school, this ought to have been brought forward at the RPD hearing. It is unfortunate if the Appellant misunderstood the question, however, there is no doubt that there was no evidence that family members had incurred any harm or threats. Moreover, if the Appellant's son had, in fact, been expelled from school, it was incumbent upon the Appellant to proffer some corroborative evidence to support this allegation. In the absence of this corroborative evidence, given the RPD's finding, the RAD concludes that the Appellant's son, the minor Appellant was not expelled from school. Summons

The Appellant submits that it was erroneous for the RPD, first acknowledging that the PSB are not consistent in issuing summons, to then come to a conclusion that they would likely issue one if the PSB were in pursuit.

Though the documentary evidence also states that the issuance of the summons is not uniformly carried out throughout the country, the RAD notes that in this instance, the PSB has made continued efforts to find the Appellant on 7 or 8 occasions, and has arrested the remaining four members of her Falun Gong group. Although this policy is not always implemented, it is reasonable that one would have been issued in respect of the Appellant, given that she testified that the PSB had been vigorous in their pursuit. To have allegedly attended her family home this frequently and regularly would indicate that the PSB had more than a casual interest in the Appellant, particularly given the allegation that the four group members still remain in detention. The lack of a summons or arrest warrant, when one should reasonably have been issued, damages the credibility of the Appellant. In this regard, the RAD draws a negative inference. Exit

It is submitted that the Appellant made it clear that she used the services of a smuggler to circumvent the system through the airport. This smuggler, it is argued, offered services in bribing airport officials to facilitate her movement through the airport and onto the aircraft.
It is further argued that the document evidence cited by the RPD3contains no evidence that Policenet has a database containing exits and entries into the country.

The RPD drew an adverse credibility finding based on the Appellant's ability to exit China on her own passport at a time she alleges she was wanted by the PSB. The RPD found that the Appellant exited China on her own identity document, thus confirming that the authorities were not concerned with her undermining her identity as a Falun Gong practitioner who is wanted by the PSB.

The RAD finds, after its own review and assessment of the evidence, that the documentary evidence in the record reveals that the Chinese government has a national computer network known as the Golden Shield Project,4 and the PSB has access to a national policing database, which includes information about criminal fugitives and information on passports and exit and entry. The Golden Shield incorporated extensive tracking and control mechanisms including facial recognition surveillance technology.

The RAD also notes from its own review and assessment of the evidence that the Exit and Entry Administration Law of China, which came into force on July 1, 2013, states the following:5 (...) Article 11. Chinese citizens who exit or enter China shall submit their exit/entry documents such as passports or other travel documents to the exit/entry border inspection authorities for examination, go through the prescribed formalities, and may exit or enter upon examination and approval. Article 12. Under any of the following circumstances, Chinese citizens are not allowed to exit China: (...) are suspects or defendants in criminal cases.

The Interpretation of the Supreme People's Court Concerning the Implementation of the Criminal Procedure Law provided the following guidelines: 6 [translation] (...) If a foreigner or a Chinese citizen must be prevented from leaving China at a border control station, the people's court accepting the case shall report up the hierarchy to the High People's Court, and a written notification of preventing person from departing through entry-exit port shall be issued by the Highest People's Court, and work with the public security organ of the corresponding level for handle control formalities. If the control port is not within the same province, autonomous region, or municipality directly under the central government, the public security organ in the relevant province, autonomous region, or municipality directly under the central government shall be contacted for the handle control formalities. Under emergency situations, if necessary, may first have the border control prevent departure and complete control formalities later. (China 20 Dec. 2012, Art. 404).

The RAD also notes that the documentation states that security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities (also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield).7 3. Information Sharing by Public Security Officials In 10 February 2014 correspondence with the Research Directorate, the Executive Director of the Dui Hua Foundation affirmed that airport security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities [also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield]. Similarly, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation stated that reports on "experiences of activists who have been detained while trying to board an international flight provide clear evidence that airport officials are connected to Policenet" (26 Feb. 2014). A colleague of Cao Shunli, who was also prevented from travelling to Geneva for the human rights training in September 2013, later publicized her own experience at the airport in Guangdong (HRIC 11 Oct. 2013). According to the Laogai research Foundation, the colleague indicates that when her passport was swiped by airport authorities, scanning equipment immediately made noises alerting airport officials that she was wanted by police. She was subsequently detained in the Guangdong Baiyun Airport and told that Shanghai police would not let her leave. She was then transported from Guangdong to Shanghai for detention and questioning. This woman's experience provides concrete evidence of airport officials coordinating with police departments in tracking and detaining a political dissident. (26 Feb. 2014)8 4. Security and Exit Control Procedures The representative of the Laogai Research Foundation wrote that the Chinese government checks the passports of citizens attempting to leave the country in order to ensure that they are suitable for foreign travel. Customs officials stamp the passports of citizens approved for foreign travel. Public security officials often confiscate passports held by individuals deemed unsuitable for foreign travel. (23 Feb. 2014).9

An undated article on the website of the Ministry of Public Security, entitled: "Deepening the Implementation of the 'Golden Shield' Project" states that: all police units nationwide have access to eight public security databases, including the "National Basic Population Information Database" (China n.d.). Also accessible through the databases is information on household registration [hukou], border exit and entry, road traffic, and criminal investigations (ibid.).10

In particular, the RAD notes that the system has been used to track down Falun Gong practitioners. The Chinese economist writing in Open Magazine affirms that: ...Cisco's Policenet has been helping the [Chinese Communist Party]'s public security organs to ferret out political dissidents and Falun Gong practitioners for years (17 Feb. 2010).11

In addition, the representative of the Laogai Research Foundation provided the following information: The Golden Shield incorporates extensive tracking and control mechanisms such as real-name online registration requirements, GPS monitoring, and facial recognition surveillance technology in a multi-pronged approach to identify potentially disruptive individuals. Policenet, a component of the Golden Shield, stores a wealth of information on Chinese citizens and connects the various agencies and levels of command within the public security apparatus. This integrated system enables Chinese public security forces to effectively target and neutralize political dissidents. (26 Feb. 2014)12

According to a Canadian embassy official in Beijing, a traveller will pass through four points: a check-in counter, a security checkpoint for entry into the airport's secure zone, departure immigration where border authorities are located, and the boarding gate; at each of the points, the traveller's passport may be checked, with scanning occurring at the check-in counter and the immigration checkpoint.13 Another source cited in the NDP, an assistant director for aviation security at the International Air Transport Association ("IATA"), indicates that three checkpoints exist, without making reference to the boarding gate, and states that a traveller's passport is checked at each of these locations.14 The IATA official also noted that specific departure procedures vary at each airport, but that the general procedures are consistent.15

The NDP also indicates that freedom to exit China is not absolute.16 Under Article 12 of the Exit and Entry Administration Law of China, exit from the country is denied under certain circumstances, including instances where the citizen does not hold valid exit documents, or is a suspect or defendant in a criminal case.17 Chinese border authorities have also effectively implemented exit control measures, although there are isolated incidents of successful evasion18 and it appears that the database is automatically searched when border authorities scan a passport.19

The RAD also finds that the Appellant's evidence of the smuggler was vague and lacking detail. The RAD finds it is reasonable to expect that an individual who is trying to avoid arrest and detention by leaving the country would want to know what services the smuggler she was engaging was able to provide and what steps would be taken to ensure her safe passage from China. The RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that she was aware of the risks of engaging in Falun Gong and only joined after she was confident there were security measures in place to ensure her safety. In light of this, and given her apparent confidence and sophistication, it is reasonable to expect she would seek similar assurance from the snakehead.

The RAD notes, however, the conclusions drawn about the plausibility of the Appellant being able to leave China on her own passport in the present case is based on recent information in the NDP. The RAD notes that in 10 February 2014 correspondence with the Research Directorate, the Executive Director of the Dui Hua Foundation affirmed that "airport security officials have access to the Public Security Bureau of China's online database of citizens who have been convicted of crimes or are wanted by the authorities [also known as Policenet or the Golden Shield]." and that there is concrete evidence of airport officials coordinating with police departments in tracking and detaining wanted persons.20

The RAD finds that evidence reveals that the Golden Shield system is an intensive security apparatus that is far-reaching and encompassing. The RAD finds that given the importance of this system to Chinese authorities in monitoring its citizens, it is reasonable to expect that the use of the apparatus is also monitored and that there are redundant systems in place to prevent the system from being compromised by a single individual. In addition, the RAD notes that the Appellant has alleged that the PSB have continued to pursue her after her departure from China. The RAD finds that this allegation undermines the suggestion that her name was somehow removed from computer system.

The RAD also notes that the evidence suggests that the Appellant's passport was examined numerous times. The RAD finds it highly improbable that the smuggler would have the prior knowledge of who to bribe in order to facilitate safe travel through each checkpoint. The RAD also notes that Article 51 of the Exit and Entry Administration Law of the People's Republic of China requires that companies involved in the transportation of goods and passengers in and out of Chinese ports must declare information on the goods and passengers in advance of their departure or entry to the country.21 Chinese border authorities are provided what is described as "advance passenger information" on arriving and departing passengers.22 This information contains a number of details of that passenger, including full name, date of birth, gender, nationality, country of residence, travel document type, and passport number, expiry date, and issuing country.23 With respect to flights into the country, it appears that China maintains a "stop list," which bars the passenger from boarding the aircraft; however, the NDP remains silent on whether a similar list exists for outbound flights.24 In any event, it is evident that border authorities are provided detailed information on the passengers aboard outbound flights.

The RAD finds that, in light of the Appellant's allegation that the PSB have continued to show interest in vigorously pursuing her, it is reasonable to expect that the local authorities would have entered her information into the database to further their efforts to apprehend her.

The RAD is aware that there is evidence in the record which establishes that there is corruption in China. However, the RAD notes that the very comprehensive Australian Refugee Review Tribunal Background paper on official Corruption in China and the other objective evidence in the record makes no mention that corruption extends to the airport security apparatus. The objective evidence states that corrupt practices are evident in many areas of Chinese society but most sources agree that corruption problems are concentrated in sectors with extensive state involvement, such as construction, land use, infrastructure, property development and banking. The former Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao said in March 2012 that "corruption tends to occur frequently in departments that possess great power and in areas where the management of funds is centralised."25

The RAD does not accept the Appellant's evidence as credible with respect to her passage through an international airport, while wanted by the PSB. The RAD finds that the objective evidence concerning the Golden Shield and other border controls in place in China is compelling and convincing. While it might be possible for a smuggler to bypass some of the security controls, the RAD finds that, based on the evidence in the record, it is highly unlikely that the Appellant could have bypassed all of the security controls in place. The RAD finds, on the basis of its analysis, that the Appellant's allegation that she was wanted by the police is not credible.

The RAD's finding in this regard is supported in the Refugee Appeal Division decision of X (Re), 2015 CanLII 72857 (CA IRB), addressing similar circumstances: API [advance passenger information] requirements which have been in effect for years, in conjunction with the highly effective Golden Shield program, makes it, on a balance of probabilities, unlikely a wanted person could depart China from an international airport using a passport with his own name, date of birth, and photograph in it. The likelihood of bribing so many people as would be involved in a person's departure is miniscule. From the person selling the ticket, to the check in counter, to the security checkpoint, the customs and immigration people onto the person who checks the Boarding pass, all of these people may be randomly in place and make it nearly impossible for anyone to know who to bribe at what point. It is simply implausible that a wanted man will escape China on his own legitimate documents.26

After its own review and assessment of the evidence, the RAD agrees with the RPD's findings and does not find it credible or plausible that the Appellant was able to leave China on her own passport after coming to the attention of the PSB. The RAD further finds that this undermines the credibility of the Appellant's allegations that she was being pursued by the PSB because of her Falun Gong activities. Sur Place

The Appellant argues that the RPD dismissed her knowledge of FG as having being learned here in Canada for the purpose of the hearing. It is submitted that the RPD imposed an unrealistically high standard of knowledge on the Appellant. Moreover, it is argued that the standard of proof must not be confused with the legal test to be met, which was recognized in Adjei27 and that the relevant provision is now section 96 of the IRPA.

The RAD finds that it was open to the RPD to import its credibility findings from the testimony surrounding the Appellant's alleged Falun Gong practice in China. The RAD concurs with the RPD that the Appellant has not provided sufficient credible evidence upon which to establish her identity as a genuine Falun Gong practitioner, and therefore, she is not wanted by the PSB. In this regard, the Federal Court in Jiang,28 stated that the Board must be entitled to import its credibility findings into its assessment of an applicant's sur place claim. The RAD finds that the RPD's finding in regard to the Appellant's sur place claim is absent of any error. Moreover, upon review of the audio recording, the RAD finds that there was insufficient credible evidence upon which to find that the Chinese authorities would be aware of the Appellant's alleged activities here in Canada.

After conducting an independent assessment of the entire record, the RAD finds that the Appellant has not provided credible or trustworthy evidence to support her allegations of FG practice and the PSB being in pursuit as a result. The RAD concurs with the findings of the RPD that this conclusion is based on a lack of a summons, lack of detail with respect to the detention of the co-practitioners or any ill harm to family members, the Appellant's ability to leave China without being detected, and inconsistent evidence with respect to her practice of FG.
For these reasons, the RAD finds that the Appellant and her minor child are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection.

Pursuant to subsection 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD. This appeal is dismissed.
